Stated Claim / Post Context:
Karoline Leavitt says press secretary job 'obviously was not for' Katie Zacharia as she helps Trump find replacement

Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt is keeping it blunt when describing her successor, Katie Zacharia's brief stint in the job.

Actual Article Body:
By SAMANTHA LOREN, US POLITICAL REPORTER

Published:  05:53 AEDT, 23 October 2026   |  Updated:  08:23 AEDT, 23 October 2026

Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt unleashed a sharp and blunt verdict on Katie Zacharia's week-long stint in her old job.

'The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well,' Leavitt told Fox News Digital backstage at a Turning Point USA campus tour stop at California Polytechnic State University.

She added that President Trump was continuing to consider his options for the position and that she had offered her expertise to help him find the right replacement.

Leavitt, who served as President Donald Trump's first press secretary during his second term, opened up about the preparation that went into her first press briefing to the crowd of campus students.

'I prepared like heck for that first briefing,' Leavitt said.

'I poured myself into my preparation. I read, I studied, I talked to every Cabinet member, I talked to the president. I just absorbed as much information as this noggin up here could.'

The comments come after Zacharia's tenure ended just days after she took the White House briefing-room podium for the first time with a wobbly performance.

Trump announced Zacharia's appointment on October 9, after first contacting her about the role on October 7.

'The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well,' former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said about her successor, Katie Zacharia

Zacharia's debut briefing lasted just 14 minutes, taking questions from only three reporters

Trump announced Leavitt's appointment on November 15, 2024, while he was still president-elect. She didn't deliver her first White House press briefing until January 28, 2025, giving her more than two months between the announcement and her debut

She officially began the job on October 12 and faced reporters for the first time the following day.

Her debut briefing lasted just 14 minutes, with questions from only three reporters.

Trump subsequently praised her performance, telling reporters: 'I thought she did excellent. She did very good.'

But the appointment quickly became a talking point, with questions raised about Zacharia's limited preparation time and her experience handling the White House press corps.

Zacharia also faced questions over her legal credentials after it was brought to light that she had failed California's bar exam in 2011.

She then moved to Beijing with her husband and worked at a Chinese law firm.

Despite never passing the bar exam, Zacharia frequently appeared on news channels as a legal analyst, offering commentary on legal and political issues while identifying herself as a lawyer.

Zacharia's rocky debut was followed by an uncomfortable appearance on Sean Hannity's Fox News show on October 15, just hours before she was pushed out of the job the following day.

Hannity delivered a notably tough grilling, confronting her over her widely criticized briefing, pressing her on why she had repeatedly described herself as a lawyer despite failing the California bar exam.

He challenged her explanation for the short briefing, asking: 'Why only three questions in 14 minutes?' before warning her that the White House briefing room would 'never be a friendly room to you.'

Zacharia defended herself by blaming the whirlwind hiring process and lack of preparation time, but the combative interview added to the scrutiny surrounding her brief tenure.

As Leavitt reflects upon her first briefing, the lack of preparation on Zacharia's end gave a major disadvantage.

Trump announced Leavitt's appointment on November 15, 2024, while he was still president-elect.

She didn't deliver her first White House press briefing until January 28, 2025, giving her more than two months between the announcement and her debut.

Leavitt, who was 27 when she took the job, became the youngest White House press secretary in history.

Her first briefing lasted around 46 minutes, during which she took questions on the administration's agenda and media access.

Leavitt announced her departure from the role on August 12, attributing the decision to wanting to spend more time with her growing family.

Trump praised Leavitt as one of his most trusted aides and said he understood her decision to spend more time with her family.

She also agreed to remain an outside adviser to the president.

Now, however, Leavitt is preparing for a return to the national spotlight.

Fox News announced on October 5 that she would join the network as an on-air contributor, providing political analysis and commentary across its platforms beginning November 1.

Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, in a Fox News Digital exclusive, offers candid verdict on successor's short-lived stint as Trump's press secretary and shares that she's advising the president as he picks another successor.

MANCHESTER, N.H. - Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt says she is helping President Donald Trump choose his next press secretary after his first pick for the job lasted just five days.

"I've offered my help to the president to help him select someone who can serve him and the country well," Leavitt said Wednesday evening in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital.

Leavitt served as Trump's press secretary from the start of the president's second term until Aug. 27, when she stepped down from the demanding role to spend more time with her two young children, including a daughter who was born in May.

Her successor, political commentator Katie Zacharia, took over earlier this month, but lasted just five days in the role, making her the shortest-serving White House press secretary in U.S. history.

TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY OUT OF A JOB JUST DAYS AFTER ROCKY DEBUT

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia arrives to a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"White House press secretary is a tough job. I know that because I did it, obviously for almost two years, and many people say it's one of the hardest jobs in politics," Leavitt emphasized.

She noted that the job "takes a lot of preparation and sometimes you don't know how someone will perform until they go out there."

"We wish Katie the best. The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well," Leavitt added.

When it comes to whom Trump will choose next for the position, Leavitt said the president "is continuing to look over options. There's a lot of people who want that job. It's an amazing job. It provides you with incredible opportunities."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

President Donald Trump, joined by White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, speaks to reporters before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Aug. 21, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

Asked what advice she's offered to Trump, Leavitt said, "I'll keep my private counsel to the president private, but I do obviously talk to him about what the job entails, and he knows it very well."

"Nobody understands the press better than Donald Trump. He knows he needs someone who is tough, who is smart, who understands his policies, who is loyal, and who can go out there and put up a fight," she added.

Leavitt, a New Hampshire native, served as an intern in the Trump White House after graduating from Saint Anselm College in 2019. She later became an assistant White House press secretary at the end of Trump's first term.

After Trump's defeat in the 2020 presidential election, Leavitt worked as communications director for Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik of New York. She then served as spokeswoman for the Trump-aligned super PAC MAGA Inc. before taking over as press secretary for Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.

After being named White House press secretary following the 2024 election, Leavitt made history as the youngest person ever in the role.

DEMOCRACY â26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Karoline Leavitt, on the campaign trail in Londonderry, New Hampshire on Sept. 8, 2022, as she runs for Congress. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Leavitt also ran for Congress in 2022, winning a heavily contested GOP nomination in New Hampshire's 1st District before losing the general election to incumbent Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas.

Asked if she might make another run for public office in her home state when Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan is up for re-election in 2028, Leavitt quickly said, "No, I'm all set. I don't have any plans to run for office in the near future at all, or in the future at all."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I am home with my family, and we're really excited about that," she explained. "Right now I'm really focused on being a wife and a mother to my two very young children. That's why I made the decision to leave Washington. So we're just happy to be home and enjoying the ride."

Leavitt officially becomes a Fox News contributor at the start of November.
